newsitem.title: UK: British wife loses bid to use dead husband's sperm.
newsitem.headline: British wife loses bid to use dead husband's sperm.

text.p: A young British widow lost her battle on Thursday to have a baby through artificial insemination using her dead husband's sperm.

In a case which has sparked intense debate, Judge Stephen Brown, president of the London High Court's family division, supported a refusal by the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority (HEFA) to allow the procedure.
The regulatory body prevented Diane Blood, 30, from using her husband's sperm because he had not given his written consent for its use before he died in March 1995 from meningitis.
"I have found this to be a most anxious and moving case," Brown told the court. "My heart goes out to this applicant who wishes to preserve an essential part of her late beloved husband."
Blood wept quietly in court as Brown announced the decision which prevents her from taking her husband's sperm to Belgium or the United States where doctors had already agreed to treat her.
The HEFA had argued it would have been illegal under the 1990 Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act to allow the procedure in Britain or abroad without the husband's written consent.
Blood claimed she and her huband had been trying for a year to have a baby. The sperm was taken from him at her request while he was on a life-support system in a coma.
Her lawyer, Anthony Lester, had argued that to destroy the sperm would be "undeniably wanton".
"It is a crucial part of her husband. His genetic material is alive and in storage," he had told the court during the three-day hearing.

"This is not a case about disregarding the wishes of the deceased husband. It is a case of furthering those wishes. It is a case about advances in medical science being able to help his widow t have the child which they both so much wanted."
Pavid Pannick, the lawyer representing the HEFA, had told the court that while it "profoundly sympathised" with Blood under the law written consent was required.
"The authority is attempting in good faith to comply with what we understood to be the views of parliament in this sensitive and developing field," he argued.
Blood, who married in 1991, had the support of both her parents and her husband's parents in her fight to try to have his baby.
